statement: A normalizing constant (normalizing factor) is a constant c by which an everywhere-nonnegative function p, whose integral (or sum) over its domain is finite, is multiplied so that the result integrates (or sums) to 1. Continuous case: given p(x) ≥ 0 with c = ∫ p(x) dx < ∞, define φ(x) = (1/c) p(x), so ∫ φ(x) dx = 1 and φ is a probability density function. Discrete case: given p(n) ≥ 0 with c = Σ_n p(n) < ∞, define φ(n) = (1/c) p(n), so Σ_n φ(n) = 1 and φ is a probability mass function.

symbols.meaning: everywhere-nonnegative function with finite integral or sum
normalizing constant, c = ∫ p(x) dx or c = Σ p(n)

symbols.dimensions: scalar function, probability density or mass function

symbols.meaning: normalizing constant in Bayes' theorem, P(D) = Σ_i P(D|H_i)P(H_i)

properties.property: For a nonnegative function p(x) with finite integral, c = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} p(x) dx, and φ(x) = p(x)/c satisfies ∫ φ(x) dx = 1, making it a probability density function. Example: p(x) = e^{-x²/2} has ∫ p dx = √(2π), so φ(x) = (1/√(2π)) e^{-x²/2} is the standard normal density.
properties.why: direct consequence of the definition applied to the Gaussian function

properties.property: The same construction applies to discrete nonnegative functions: since Σ_{n=0}^∞ λⁿ/n! = e^λ, the normalizing constant is e^λ and f(n) = λⁿ e^{-λ}/n! is a probability mass function (the Poisson distribution).
properties.why: discrete analogue of the continuous case, sum replaces integral

properties.property: In Bayes' theorem, the posterior is proportional to prior × likelihood: P(H_0|D) ∝ P(D|H_0)P(H_0). Because Σ_i P(H_i|D) = 1, the normalizing constant is P(D) = Σ_i P(D|H_i)P(H_i) (or the corresponding integral over a continuum of hypotheses), giving P(H_0|D) = P(D|H_0)P(H_0) / P(D).
properties.why: posterior probabilities over mutually exclusive hypotheses must sum to 1

properties.property: If the unnormalized function depends on parameters, the normalizing constant is itself a function of those parameters; in statistical mechanics, the normalizing constant of the Boltzmann distribution is called the partition function.
properties.why: stated directly as a note in the source

properties.property: The concept extends beyond probability: the constant that scales a Legendre polynomial so its value at 1 equals 1 is a normalizing constant, and orthonormal functions are normalized so that ⟨f_i, f_j⟩ = δ_{i,j} with respect to an inner product.
properties.why: non-probabilistic uses given explicitly in the source

assumptions.breaks_when: p takes negative values, so no scaling makes it a valid density/mass function

assumptions.assumption: the integral or sum of p over its domain is finite
assumptions.breaks_when: the integral/sum diverges, so no finite normalizing constant exists (improper distribution)

failure_modes.signature: ∫ p(x) dx or Σ p(n) is infinite
failure_modes.cause: the unnormalized function does not decay fast enough / has unbounded mass

failure_modes.mode: normalizing constant P(D) is intractable to compute directly
failure_modes.signature: posterior can only be evaluated up to proportionality; direct summation or integration over hypotheses is infeasible
failure_modes.cause: high-dimensional or continuous hypothesis space, requiring estimation methods such as bridge sampling, naive Monte Carlo, the generalized harmonic mean estimator, or importance sampling
